candidates.title: Sip or gulp: which one doubles brain freeze?
candidates.opening_promise: Sip or gulp? Two experiments settle it.

thumbnail.concept: one huge glass of ice water with a straw; 'HALF GOT IT' teases the gulp result without naming the winner

candidates.description: Gulping ice water gave half of 77 volunteers brain freeze; an ice cube on the palate, one in eight. A school trial found the same with fast ice cream.
candidates.rationale: the video's own question; the thumbnail adds the evidence hint

candidates.title: Brain freeze isn't your brain freezing
candidates.opening_promise: Brain freeze starts in your mouth, not your brain.

thumbnail.concept: big wincing face, pain zigzag on the forehead, arrow up from the mouth

candidates.description: Cold on the roof of your mouth sets it off, and the ache shows up in your forehead. It's referred pain, and it fades within 10 minutes.

candidates.title: Eating fast doubles your odds of brain freeze
candidates.opening_promise: One habit doubles your odds of brain freeze.

thumbnail.concept: giant cone with speed lines; the two trial numbers

candidates.description: In a randomised trial with 145 students, eating ice cream in under 5 seconds caused brain freeze in 27%, versus 13% for slow eaters.

candidates.title: Ice water vs an ice cube: which triggers brain freeze?
candidates.opening_promise: Same cold, very different odds of brain freeze.

thumbnail.concept: one giant ice cube, 'ONLY 12%' (the cube result; the gulp result is the reveal)

candidates.description: In one experiment, gulped ice water triggered brain freeze in half of 77 people; an ice cube held on the palate in one in eight.
